title: Probabilistic Error Cancellation for Single-Mode Gottesman-Kitaev-Preskill Codes
abstract: In order to solve practical problems on a quantum computer, it is necessary to use fault-tolerant quantum error correction schemes to overcome noise: the errors arising from imperfections in physical components. The Gottesman-Kitaev-Preskill (GKP) code aims at achieving this in a hardware efficient manner by encoding finite-dimensional logical subspaces in the Hilbert space of one or more continuous variable modes. In near term implementations, however, it is not feasible to eliminate errors entirely, so it is natural to also employ alternative error mitigation techniques together with error correction. In this work, we study a quantum error mitigation method known as probabilistic error cancellation in the context of the GKP code. We compare Steane-type and teleportation-based GKP error correction, and calculate the sampling overheads associated with the technique for square and hexagonal GKP codes. We employ the stabilizer subsystem decomposition for GKP codes to obtain an effective logical channel for noisy operations that is used to express the ideal one of a target logical unitary. We consider noise from finite squeezing on the data and the two ancilla modes, needed for error correction, and examine the relationship between the sampling overhead and the noise for different decoding methods. Our results are calculated for single- and two-qubit GKP Clifford gates and one round of error correction, and show the nontrivial combination of error correction and mitigation in continuous variable codes.
summary: This paper investigates combining Quantum Error Correction (QEC) with Quantum Error Mitigation (QEM) for continuous variable quantum computation using the GKP code. It specifically analyzes the overhead required by Probabilistic Error Cancellation (PEC) when applied after standard GKP error correction protocols. The results provide quantitative estimates for noise resilience in these advanced CV quantum computing schemes.
main_problem: The paper addresses the need for fault-tolerant quantum computation by studying the combination of Quantum Error Correction (QEC) with Quantum Error Mitigation (QEM) techniques.
main_result: It quantifies the sampling overhead associated with using Probabilistic Error Cancellation (PEC) alongside GKP error correction, demonstrating a nontrivial interplay between these two error handling methods in continuous variable codes.
method: The authors use the stabilizer subsystem decomposition to characterize the effective logical channel and employ PEC, which involves decomposing an ideal gate into noisy basis operations to estimate expectation values.
model_or_system: The system is based on continuous variable (CV) quantum information encoded using the Gottesman-Kitaev-Preskill (GKP) code, analyzed for both square and hexagonal lattice structures.
key_observables: Sampling overhead ($C_{em}$), noise covariance matrices ($\Sigma_{	ext{QEC},\Lambda}$), and the effective logical channel.
important_parameters: GKP squeezing parameter ($\Delta$), noise parameters (mean $\mu$ and covariance $\Sigma$ for Gaussian Random Displacement noise), and the type of GKP gate (single- or two-qubit Clifford gates).
main_assumptions: The analysis assumes noise is modeled by Gaussian Random Displacement (GRD) noise and relies on the stabilizer subsystem decomposition to map the noisy process to an effective logical channel.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the quantum circuits for both Steane-type and teleportation-based GKP error correction for a single mode, and the appendices detail the mathematical derivations for noise propagation in both schemes.
paper_structure: The paper builds from defining the GKP code structure (Zak basis completeness) to analyzing the noise propagation through two distinct QEC protocols (Steane vs. Teleportation), and finally applying PEC to estimate the overhead associated with mitigating these residual errors.
why_interesting: This work is highly relevant for theoretical physicists working on quantum optics and open quantum systems as it provides concrete, quantitative methods for dealing with realistic noise sources in continuous variable quantum computation architectures.
